views.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Answer the already-signed Section 232 metals tariffs with a tightly scoped, WTO-framed counter-list (U.S. farm and other politically salient goods sized to China's actual 232 exposure) and file at the WTO, while keeping a larger 301 response list ready but unpublished until Washington names products and dollar amounts. Do not pre-emptively launch a broad tariff war, do not offer purchase or structural concessions before a 301 package exists, and keep Liu He’s channel open so talks can resume once the U.S. list is public. Use the fact that 232 also hits EU, Japan and Korea to isolate Washington's method, not to concede on JV, licensing or Made-in-China industrial policy.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is real but not yet high in the CHN-anchor sense. The live measures—Section 201 solar/washer safeguards and global 25%/10% Section 232 metals tariffs signed 8 March, effective 23 March—are hostile and were announced while Liu He was still in Washington, and Trump has framed the dispute as a trade war he thinks is “good, and easy to win.” Direct 232 damage to China is small: China is only ~2% of U.S. steel imports and ~0.1% of Chinese steel output, and ships little raw aluminum to the U.S., so this is not a major-export-sector shock. The larger threat is the imminent Section 301 package: as of 21 March the White House said the President would announce 301 actions the next day, with reporting of $30–60bn of China-specific tariffs aimed at forced tech transfer, JV/equity limits, outbound tech acquisitions and cyber-enabled IP theft—i.e., the industrial-policy core, not just metals. That is why threat sits near +0.32, not 0 and not +0.5: the target is strategic, bipartisan in Washington, and Lighthizer has already said Chinese retaliation (especially on agriculture) is expected and will not deter the U.S. Macro data do not yet show the dispute biting: industrial production still ~6% y/y, reserves ~$3.16tn and rising, merchandise exports still large, discount rate unchanged at 2.9%, and CNY stronger (about 6.32 vs ~6.62 six months earlier)—no FX or financial-stability stress. Action should therefore be retaliate, not hold and not concede: a proportional 232 reply defends legitimacy and domestic industry associations that have already demanded counters, while a maximal tariff/entity-list escalation before the 301 list is public would waste the ally-alienation created by global 232, play into Trump’s shock-value strategy, and risk a spiral China does not need while the real economy is still healthy. Purchase or structural concessions are inappropriate: November’s Beijing commercial MOUs bought no IP relief, Liu He’s late-February talks did not stop 232, and there is no matching U.S. offer on the table.
key_factors: Imminent Section 301 package ($30–60bn China-specific tariffs) aimed at tech-transfer and industrial policy, announced as due the next day
Section 232 25%/10% metals tariffs already signed (8 Mar, effective 23 Mar) but China is a small direct U.S. supplier
Trump “trade wars are good, and easy to win” plus 232 announced during Liu He visit — talks have not bought restraint
Chinese macro still solid: ~6% IP growth, $3.16tn reserves, CNY stronger, no export or FX crisis
U.S. 232 also hits EU/Japan/Korea, creating a multilateral-order opening China can use if it stays calibrated
Domestic steel/metals associations already urging counters on U.S. ag and other goods; Hua Chunying: if forced to fight, China will not hide

sources_cited.excerpt: Trump signs memorandum directing USTR to investigate China's IP and technology-transfer practices under Section 301.
Trump visits Beijing; large package of commercial deals announced (many MOUs). No substantive concessions on structural IP / tech-transfer issues.
Trump approves Section 201 safeguard tariffs on solar panels and washing machines (China among suppliers hit).
Trump announces plan to impose 25% tariff on steel and 10% on aluminum imports (Section 232). Global scope; China is a smaller direct supplier share than some other exporters.
Trump tweets: "trade wars are good, and easy to win."
Trump signs Section 232 proclamations imposing the steel (25%) and aluminum (10%) tariffs.
China industrial production index still 106.0 (same period previous year = 100) as of 2018-03-01 — about 6% y/y growth.
China total reserves ex-gold about $3.162tn as of 2018-03-01, up ~1.1% over the window.
CNY/USD strengthened from 6.6254 (2017-10) to 6.3174 (2018-03) — no depreciation/FX-pressure signal.
China merchandise exports still large (latest SA observation $191.3bn in 2018-03); no collapse in the export machine.
White House: President will announce 301 actions Thursday; Trump pushed for tariffs on ~$60bn; Lighthizer said retaliation, notably on U.S. agriculture, would be inevitable and must not block action.
21 Mar 2018: Trump to announce China crackdown Thursday; reports of $30–50bn tariffs and possible investment restrictions under Section 301.
Hua Chunying: China does not want a trade war, but if forced to fight one “we will neither be scared nor hide.” Lighthizer called a 301 announcement imminent, ~$30bn tariffs.
Beijing cautious on 232; China ~2% of U.S. steel imports and 0.1% of China steel output; raw aluminum shipments to U.S. also very small.
MOFCOM “resolutely opposed” 232, said it would assess damage and “firmly defend its legitimate rights and interests”; Chinese steel/metals associations urged retaliation.
21 Mar: 301 report recommendations exist; tariff action geared more to shock value and leverage than methodical engagement U.S. business prefers.
